questions.text: Philippine timber stress groups rank species by structural capacity. Which of the following is a Group I (highest strength) species?

options.text: Yakal
Narra
Lauan
White Lauan

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: Yakal is classified as Group I (highest), along with Molave, Ipil, Guijo, and Mangkono. Group I species have the highest allowable bending and compression stresses.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: Identify the correct stress group for each species: Narra, Lauan, Apitong.

options.text: Narra: Group II, Lauan: Group III, Apitong: Group I
Narra: Group I, Lauan: Group III, Apitong: Group III
Narra: Group I, Lauan: Group III, Apitong: Group IV
Narra: Group II, Lauan: Group IV, Apitong: Group II

rationale.a: Apitong is Group III, not Group I.
rationale.c: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.d: Narra is Group II, not Group I. Apitong is Group II, not Group IV.
rationale.correct: Narra (Group II), Lauan (Group III), Apitong (Group II). Apitong and Narra are both high-capacity species in Group II; Lauan is moderate capacity (Group III).
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: A structural specification states 'Hardboard (density ≥497 kg/m³) as primary shear wall backing.' An engineer proposes using fiberboard (280 kg/m³) instead to reduce cost. What compliance issue exists?

options.text: Fiberboard does not meet the density threshold (≥497 kg/m³ for hardboard). The substitution violates the specification and is non-compliant; hardboard (or specification modification) is required.
Density is the only specification criterion; any timber-based product of equivalent thickness is acceptable, provided it meets other structural requirements
Fiberboard can substitute for hardboard if the thickness is increased by 50% to compensate for lower density, ensuring structural integrity
Hardboard and fiberboard are identical products; the terminology difference is cosmetic, with no impact on performance

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: The specification is explicit: hardboard ≥497 kg/m³. Density is not the only criterion; product category is definitive.
rationale.d: Thickness adjustment does not alter the material's internal structure, modulus, or water-resistance—all properties engineered into hardboard versus fiberboard.
rationale.correct: Hardboard is defined as density ≥497 kg/m³. Fiberboard (>160 to <497 kg/m³) is a separate product category with different mechanical properties. The specification requires hardboard; fiberboard does not meet the definition and is non-compliant.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: A design uses Apitong lumber but the project location is remote and Apitong is unavailable. The contractor proposes substituting White Lauan of the same grade and dimensions. What design issue arises?

options.text: White Lauan is Group III (moderate capacity); Apitong is Group II. The allowable stresses are significantly different. The beam must be re-designed or rejected.
Apitong and White Lauan have similar allowable stresses; substitution is acceptable if grade and dimensions match.
White Lauan has higher density and strength than Apitong; the substitution is superior and should be approved.
Grade is the only factor in stress assignment; species group does not affect allowable stresses.

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: Groups define distinct stress ranges. Same grade does not mean same allowable stress across groups.
rationale.d: White Lauan is lower strength than Apitong, not higher.
rationale.correct: Apitong (Group II) has significantly higher allowable bending (Fb) and compression stresses than White Lauan (Group IV). Substitution without re-design violates the basis of the original design and is non-compliant.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: A timber grade schedule specifies 'No. 1 Common, 50×200 mm nominal.' What are the actual dimensions used in design calculations?

options.text: 50 × 200 mm (nominal equals actual in metric conversion)
Approximately 38 × 189 mm (surfaced from nominal)
Approximately 44 × 194 mm (standard Australian sizing)
Actual dimensions must be measured on-site; nominal is not used.

rationale.a: Nominal = actual is incorrect. Surfacing always reduces dimensions by 10–15%.
rationale.c: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.d: Australian standards use different nominal/actual conversions; Philippine grading uses the 50→38, 200→189 pattern.
rationale.correct: Nominal 50×200 mm timber is surfaced (milled) to approximately 38×189 mm actual. This reduction accounts for planing, finishing, and knot-trimming. Actual dimensions are required for all section properties (S, I, A).
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: A timber column is designed using Group II species (Narra), Select Structural grade, with Fb = 12 MPa. The project budget requires substitution to a lower grade (No. 1 Common) of the same species and dimensions. What is the design consequence?

options.text: Fb value will decrease (typically by 10–15%) because No. 1 Common permits larger knots and defects than Select Structural. The column design must be re-analyzed or reinforced.
Fb remains identical because Narra (Group II) has the same allowable stress regardless of grade, which simplifies the substitution process
No. 1 Common has higher Fb than Select Structural; the substitution improves capacity and is acceptable without re-design, contrary to typical expectations
Grade affects appearance only; structural properties depend on species and dimensions alone, which means the substitution has no impact on structural integrity

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: Grade directly affects allowable stress within the same species. Fb is not fixed for a species; it is a function of both species and grade.
rationale.d: No. 1 Common does not improve capacity; it reduces it due to larger permitted defects.
rationale.correct: Within the same species and group, grade determines the specific allowable stress level. Select Structural (best) has higher Fb than No. 1 Common (middle grade). A design using Select Structural cannot be transferred to No. 1 Common without re-analysis.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: A timber joists are specified as 'Green Yakal, Group I, Select Structural.' Explain why moisture content affects the allowable bending stress (Fb).

options.text: Green timber (≥19% moisture content) has reduced stiffness and strength; design tables provide lower Fb values for green timber than for kiln-dried (≤15% MC) to account for this loss.
Green timber has higher Fb values because moisture increases elastic modulus, which is a common misconception in structural engineering
Moisture content does not affect Fb; all Group I Select Structural timber has the same allowable stress regardless of MC, which is contrary to standard engineering practices
Green timber must be excluded from design; only kiln-dried timber is permitted, as per the latest amendments to the building code regarding structural timber use

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: Moisture reduces stiffness and strength, not increases it.
rationale.d: Many applications accept green timber; the allowable stress is simply reduced to account for the moisture penalty.
rationale.correct: Green timber has higher moisture content, which reduces the wood's stiffness, strength, and modulus. Design tables apply a moisture adjustment factor (typically 1.0–0.9) to Fb for green vs. dry conditions. Fb(green) < Fb(dry).
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: A joist specification requires actual dimensions. If nominal 2×10 Lauan (Group III, No. 1 Common) joists are delivered, what are the approximate actual dimensions, and which are used in the design?

options.text: Nominal 2×10 is approximately 38×240 mm actual. Actual dimensions are used in design calculations for section properties.
Nominal and actual are the same in modern Philippine timber; no conversion is necessary, as the industry standards have unified these measurements
Nominal 2×10 equals 50×250 mm actual; nominal is used in design because it represents the full-size product, ensuring consistency across projects
The actual dimensions cannot be determined without physical measurement; nominal must be used as a proxy, which is a common practice in preliminary design stages

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: Nominal and actual differ by 10–15% due to surfacing; conversion tables are standardized.
rationale.d: Nominal 2 is not 50 mm; the conversion is 2 in. ≈ 38 mm (not 50 mm). Nominal is never used in design calculations.
rationale.correct: Nominal 2 inches ≈ 38 mm (actual), nominal 10 inches ≈ 240 mm (actual). Allowance is made for surfacing and trimming. All section properties (S, I, A, c) are calculated using actual dimensions.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: Fiberboard has a density of 280 kg/m³. Explain why fiberboard at this density cannot replace solid lumber as a primary load-bearing beam.

options.text: Fiberboard lacks the structural modulus and shear strength of solid lumber; its low density and engineered composition limit it to non-primary-load paths like infill, backing, or insulation.
Fiberboard is only used for thermal insulation; its mechanical properties are deliberately minimized to reduce weight and cost.
Fiberboard's density is too high; it should be replaced with hardboard (≥497 kg/m³) for structural use, which is a common misconception
Fiberboard is acceptable for primary beams if thickness is doubled to compensate for lower density, which is not a recommended practice

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: Fiberboard does have some strength; the issue is that its strength is insufficient for primary structural duty, not that it is intentionally weak.
rationale.d: Hardboard (≥497 kg/m³) is denser but is still not suitable for primary beams. Hardboard is also an engineered product, not a structural member.
rationale.correct: Fiberboard (>160 to <497 kg/m³) is a composite product with lower modulus of elasticity and shear strength per unit volume than solid sawn timber. Its engineered structure is optimized for insulation and backing, not primary bending members.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: A timber beam is graded as 'Select Structural, No. 1 Common, and No. 2 Common' in the same size. Which grade permits the largest knots and defects?

options.text: No. 2 Common (lowest grade among the three listed)
No. 1 Common (middle grade), allowing moderate knots and defects but not as large as No. 2 Common
Select Structural (highest grade), which permits only minimal knots and defects, ensuring structural integrity
All three grades have identical knot limits; only color differs, which is not a standard grading practice

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: No. 1 Common is higher than No. 2; it has stricter knot limits.
rationale.d: Select Structural has the tightest defect limits of all three.
rationale.correct: No. 2 Common is the lowest grade among these three and allows the largest knots, widest checks, and most visible defects. Allowable stresses are correspondingly reduced.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.
